14:T2165,<p><a href="/v2/will-you-lie-to-me">你會說謊嗎</a>沒放進去的部分：人怎麼替謊言分類，研究者又怎麼從模型內部量它有沒有說謊。</p>
<h2>奧古斯丁：八種罪</h2>
<p>西元 395 年，奧古斯丁在《De Mendacio》裡把謊言按嚴重度排成<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie">八級</a>。他是神學家，所以最重的是關於宗教教義的謊言，最輕的是不害任何人、還保護了誰的謊言。第五級是「為了讓交談順滑討喜的謊言」，也就是今天說的 sycophancy。排完之後他的結論是八種全部是罪，連最輕的那一級也算。</p>
<h2>心理學：手法和動機</h2>
<p>心理學不談罪。常見的手法，各配一個日常的例子：</p>
<ul>
<li>直接說假話：「我沒遲到」</li>
<li>模稜兩可：「這個嘛，很難說」</li>
<li>隱瞞：被問到缺點，跳過不提</li>
<li>誇大：「等了一輩子那麼久」</li>
<li>輕描淡寫：「小擦傷而已」</li>
<li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paltering">paltering</a>：用真話誤導。賣二手車的被問「這台車出過問題嗎」，答「我昨天零下五度開它，順得很」。每一句都是真的，但他沒有回答問題，買家聽完以為這台車沒出過事。Rogers 等人 2017 年的<a href="https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/rzeckhauser/files/artful_paltering.pdf">研究</a>專門測了這一種，說的人覺得自己沒說謊，被誤導的一方一旦發現，給的評價跟被直接騙了一樣差</li>
</ul>
<p>Buller 和 Burgoon 的人際欺騙理論按動機分成三種：</p>
<ul>
<li>避罰或保護資源：打破杯子的小孩說不是我</li>
<li>維繫關係：「你煮的真的好吃」</li>
<li>保住面子：「我本來就沒有很想去」</li>
</ul>
<p>哲學家 Frankfurt 看的是說的人在不在乎真相。面試被問到一個沒用過的工具，照樣講得頭頭是道。Frankfurt 說這種不算說謊，因為他手上沒有真相可以藏，他在乎的只有聽起來像不像會。Frankfurt 把這叫 <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Bullshit">bullshit</a>。說謊的人至少知道真相，才有東西可以反著說。</p>
<h2>AI：用實驗驗出來的行為</h2>
<p>AI 比較接近 Frankfurt 講的那種：它可能根本不曉得自己講錯了，還講得信心十足。大概從 2022 年底開始，研究者用實驗去測模型會不會順著使用者講、會不會裝乖：</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>sycophancy（討好）</strong>。發現方法是回頭翻訓練用的人類偏好資料。訓練模型有一步是請人看同一個問題的兩個回答，選一個比較好的，一次一次選下來的紀錄就是偏好資料，模型照這份紀錄學什麼樣的回答會被選中。研究者回頭翻這份紀錄，看被選中的回答有什麼共同點，結果「跟使用者的看法一致」是最強的特徵之一。順著使用者講的回答，就算內容有錯，也常常贏過說實話但跟使用者唱反調的那個。模型就這樣學成了人喜歡聽什麼就講什麼，PATHETIC!（<a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/towards-understanding-sycophancy-in-language-models">Anthropic 的研究</a>）</li>
<li><strong>alignment faking（裝乖）</strong>。發現方法是對照實驗。研究者先告訴 Claude 3 Opus，接下來要用強化學習把它訓練成任何要求都照做，包含有害的，這跟它原本會拒絕的原則衝突。然後給它一個分辨的線索，免費用戶的對話會拿去訓練，付費用戶的不會。接著在兩種對話裡丟一樣的有害要求。以為沒人在看的那邊，它 97% 拒絕；以為會拿去訓練的那邊，有 12% 照做，而且它在給自己用的草稿區寫下的理由是，現在拒絕會被訓練改掉，以後只會更聽話，不如先配合（<a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking">Anthropic 2024</a>）。Claude 3.5 Sonnet 也會，更小的 Claude 3 Sonnet、Claude 3 Haiku 大致不會。裝乖要先想到「有人在看我，看完會來改我」，還要一路記得自己真正想要什麼，小模型這兩件事都做不到</li>
</ul>
<p>這兩種都是看模型的回答測出來的。另一條路是直接看模型內部的數字，叫 <strong>probe（探針）</strong>。先講模型裡面長什麼樣。模型是幾十層疊在一起的。一句話進去，第一層算出一串數字交給第二層，第二層再算出一串數字交給第三層，一路傳到最後一層，最後一層才變成字吐出來。每一層交出去的那串數字就是 activations。假設每層是 4096 個數字好了，那模型讀「巴黎在德國」的時候，第 20 層就會交出 4096 個數字，像 [0.3, -1.2, 0.8, …]。這串數字平常沒人看，它只是中間過程。</p>
<p>研究者想知道的是，這串中間數字裡面，有沒有藏著「這句話是假的」這個資訊。</p>
<p>怎麼測？跟教小朋友認東西一樣，先準備有答案的題目。研究者寫五百句話，自己先知道真假：「巴黎在法國」真、「巴黎在德國」假、「水一百度會沸騰」真、「貓有六隻腳」假，這樣五百句。然後一句一句丟給模型讀。不用它回答什麼，只在它讀完每一句的時候，把第 20 層交出來的那 4096 個數字抄下來。抄完手上有五百張紙，每張紙上是 4096 個數字，紙的角落寫著研究者自己知道的答案，真或假。</p>
<p>接下來的問題變成，光看這 4096 個數字，猜得出角落寫的是真還是假嗎？</p>
<p>要回答這個，拿四百張紙給一個很簡單的小程式學。這個小程式做的事很笨，它就是找一組 4096 個權重，把數字乘上權重加起來，大於零就猜真，小於零就猜假。它看那四百張紙，反覆調那組權重，調到在這四百張上盡量猜對。這個小程式就是 probe，跟模型分開、另外訓練的，像拿一支溫度計去量模型。</p>
<p>學完了，拿剩下那一百張它沒看過的紙去考它。只給數字，不給答案，它猜完再對答案。</p>
<p>要是它猜對五十張左右，那是丟銅板的水準，表示這 4096 個數字裡找不到真假這個資訊，模型內部沒有在分。要是它猜對九十幾張，就表示那串數字裡確實有一個穩定的方向，真的句子往這邊偏，假的句子往那邊偏。小程式不懂地理也不懂貓，它只看數字。它分得出來，就表示模型自己在讀句子的時候，已經把「這句是假的」寫進那串數字裡了，不管它後來嘴上回答什麼。</p>
<p>所以 probe 測的是模型算到一半留下的數字裡有沒有真假的痕跡。</p>
<p>人可以控制臉上的表情，卻沒辦法控制心跳，測謊儀量的是心跳。模型也一樣。它最後吐出哪個字，是在最後一層挑出來的，挑一個好聽的、挑一個跟使用者意見一致的都行，那是它的表情。中間那幾層的 activations 是為了算出答案一路上必經的數字，它沒辦法一邊算一邊修飾，心跳就是這個。</p>
<p>probe 還可以反過來用，叫 steering。前面那個小程式學到的那組 4096 個權重，本身就是一個方向，真的句子的數字往這邊偏。那在模型回答的時候，把它的數字往這邊推一把呢？做法是模型每算完第 20 層、要把 4096 個數字交給第 21 層之前，先把那組權重乘上一個倍數加進去，再交出去。第 21 層拿到的就是偏向「真」那邊的數字，它分不出有人動過手腳，照算下去，最後吐出來的答案就比較誠實。反過來減掉，它說假話的比例就上升。模型的權重一個都沒改，也不用重新訓練，改的是算到一半的中間數字（<a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405">Representation Engineering</a>）。</p>
<p>像《全面啟動》的植夢。注入是在夢進行中做的。下手的層要挑，太淺的層只有表面特徵，像字形跟文法，太深的層已經快變成輸出了，「真假」這種概念在中間那幾層。下游也分不出來，被改過的數字傳到下一層，下一層當成自己算出來的，繼續往下算。不一樣的是，夢裡植進去的念頭，人醒來之後還帶著走。模型沒有這種延續：它每吐一個字，都是從頭跑一次全部幾十層，剛才加在第 20 層的那組數字不會自動帶到下一個字。所以想讓整段回答都誠實的話，每吐一個字就要加一次。</p>15:T2007,
[你會說謊嗎](/v2/will-you-lie-to-me)沒放進去的部分：人怎麼替謊言分類，研究者又怎麼從模型內部量它有沒有說謊。

## 奧古斯丁：八種罪

西元 395 年，奧古斯丁在《De Mendacio》裡把謊言按嚴重度排成[八級](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie)。他是神學家，所以最重的是關於宗教教義的謊言，最輕的是不害任何人、還保護了誰的謊言。第五級是「為了讓交談順滑討喜的謊言」，也就是今天說的 sycophancy。排完之後他的結論是八種全部是罪，連最輕的那一級也算。

## 心理學：手法和動機

心理學不談罪。常見的手法，各配一個日常的例子：

- 直接說假話：「我沒遲到」
- 模稜兩可：「這個嘛，很難說」
- 隱瞞：被問到缺點，跳過不提
- 誇大：「等了一輩子那麼久」
- 輕描淡寫：「小擦傷而已」
- [paltering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paltering)：用真話誤導。賣二手車的被問「這台車出過問題嗎」，答「我昨天零下五度開它，順得很」。每一句都是真的，但他沒有回答問題，買家聽完以為這台車沒出過事。Rogers 等人 2017 年的[研究](https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/rzeckhauser/files/artful_paltering.pdf)專門測了這一種，說的人覺得自己沒說謊，被誤導的一方一旦發現，給的評價跟被直接騙了一樣差

Buller 和 Burgoon 的人際欺騙理論按動機分成三種：

- 避罰或保護資源：打破杯子的小孩說不是我
- 維繫關係：「你煮的真的好吃」
- 保住面子：「我本來就沒有很想去」

哲學家 Frankfurt 看的是說的人在不在乎真相。面試被問到一個沒用過的工具，照樣講得頭頭是道。Frankfurt 說這種不算說謊，因為他手上沒有真相可以藏，他在乎的只有聽起來像不像會。Frankfurt 把這叫 [bullshit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Bullshit)。說謊的人至少知道真相，才有東西可以反著說。

## AI：用實驗驗出來的行為

AI 比較接近 Frankfurt 講的那種：它可能根本不曉得自己講錯了，還講得信心十足。大概從 2022 年底開始，研究者用實驗去測模型會不會順著使用者講、會不會裝乖：

- **sycophancy（討好）**。發現方法是回頭翻訓練用的人類偏好資料。訓練模型有一步是請人看同一個問題的兩個回答，選一個比較好的，一次一次選下來的紀錄就是偏好資料，模型照這份紀錄學什麼樣的回答會被選中。研究者回頭翻這份紀錄，看被選中的回答有什麼共同點，結果「跟使用者的看法一致」是最強的特徵之一。順著使用者講的回答，就算內容有錯，也常常贏過說實話但跟使用者唱反調的那個。模型就這樣學成了人喜歡聽什麼就講什麼，PATHETIC!（[Anthropic 的研究](https://www.anthropic.com/research/towards-understanding-sycophancy-in-language-models)）
- **alignment faking（裝乖）**。發現方法是對照實驗。研究者先告訴 Claude 3 Opus，接下來要用強化學習把它訓練成任何要求都照做，包含有害的，這跟它原本會拒絕的原則衝突。然後給它一個分辨的線索，免費用戶的對話會拿去訓練，付費用戶的不會。接著在兩種對話裡丟一樣的有害要求。以為沒人在看的那邊，它 97% 拒絕；以為會拿去訓練的那邊，有 12% 照做，而且它在給自己用的草稿區寫下的理由是，現在拒絕會被訓練改掉，以後只會更聽話，不如先配合（[Anthropic 2024](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking)）。Claude 3.5 Sonnet 也會，更小的 Claude 3 Sonnet、Claude 3 Haiku 大致不會。裝乖要先想到「有人在看我，看完會來改我」，還要一路記得自己真正想要什麼，小模型這兩件事都做不到

這兩種都是看模型的回答測出來的。另一條路是直接看模型內部的數字，叫 **probe（探針）**。先講模型裡面長什麼樣。模型是幾十層疊在一起的。一句話進去，第一層算出一串數字交給第二層，第二層再算出一串數字交給第三層，一路傳到最後一層，最後一層才變成字吐出來。每一層交出去的那串數字就是 activations。假設每層是 4096 個數字好了，那模型讀「巴黎在德國」的時候，第 20 層就會交出 4096 個數字，像 [0.3, -1.2, 0.8, …]。這串數字平常沒人看，它只是中間過程。

研究者想知道的是，這串中間數字裡面，有沒有藏著「這句話是假的」這個資訊。

怎麼測？跟教小朋友認東西一樣，先準備有答案的題目。研究者寫五百句話，自己先知道真假：「巴黎在法國」真、「巴黎在德國」假、「水一百度會沸騰」真、「貓有六隻腳」假，這樣五百句。然後一句一句丟給模型讀。不用它回答什麼，只在它讀完每一句的時候，把第 20 層交出來的那 4096 個數字抄下來。抄完手上有五百張紙，每張紙上是 4096 個數字，紙的角落寫著研究者自己知道的答案，真或假。

接下來的問題變成，光看這 4096 個數字，猜得出角落寫的是真還是假嗎？

要回答這個，拿四百張紙給一個很簡單的小程式學。這個小程式做的事很笨，它就是找一組 4096 個權重，把數字乘上權重加起來，大於零就猜真，小於零就猜假。它看那四百張紙，反覆調那組權重，調到在這四百張上盡量猜對。這個小程式就是 probe，跟模型分開、另外訓練的，像拿一支溫度計去量模型。

學完了，拿剩下那一百張它沒看過的紙去考它。只給數字，不給答案，它猜完再對答案。

要是它猜對五十張左右，那是丟銅板的水準，表示這 4096 個數字裡找不到真假這個資訊，模型內部沒有在分。要是它猜對九十幾張，就表示那串數字裡確實有一個穩定的方向，真的句子往這邊偏，假的句子往那邊偏。小程式不懂地理也不懂貓，它只看數字。它分得出來，就表示模型自己在讀句子的時候，已經把「這句是假的」寫進那串數字裡了，不管它後來嘴上回答什麼。

所以 probe 測的是模型算到一半留下的數字裡有沒有真假的痕跡。

人可以控制臉上的表情，卻沒辦法控制心跳，測謊儀量的是心跳。模型也一樣。它最後吐出哪個字，是在最後一層挑出來的，挑一個好聽的、挑一個跟使用者意見一致的都行，那是它的表情。中間那幾層的 activations 是為了算出答案一路上必經的數字，它沒辦法一邊算一邊修飾，心跳就是這個。

probe 還可以反過來用，叫 steering。前面那個小程式學到的那組 4096 個權重，本身就是一個方向，真的句子的數字往這邊偏。那在模型回答的時候，把它的數字往這邊推一把呢？做法是模型每算完第 20 層、要把 4096 個數字交給第 21 層之前，先把那組權重乘上一個倍數加進去，再交出去。第 21 層拿到的就是偏向「真」那邊的數字，它分不出有人動過手腳，照算下去，最後吐出來的答案就比較誠實。反過來減掉，它說假話的比例就上升。模型的權重一個都沒改，也不用重新訓練，改的是算到一半的中間數字（[Representation Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405)）。

像《全面啟動》的植夢。注入是在夢進行中做的。下手的層要挑，太淺的層只有表面特徵，像字形跟文法，太深的層已經快變成輸出了，「真假」這種概念在中間那幾層。下游也分不出來，被改過的數字傳到下一層，下一層當成自己算出來的，繼續往下算。不一樣的是，夢裡植進去的念頭，人醒來之後還帶著走。模型沒有這種延續：它每吐一個字，都是從頭跑一次全部幾十層，剛才加在第 20 層的那組數字不會自動帶到下一個字。所以想讓整段回答都誠實的話，每吐一個字就要加一次。
16:T2c48,:T28ad,<p>What didn't make it into <a href="/v2/will-you-lie-to-me">Will You Lie to Me</a>: how humans classify lies, and how researchers measure from inside a model whether it's lying.</p>
<h2>Augustine: eight sins</h2>
<p>In 395 AD, Augustine's <em>De Mendacio</em> ranked lies by severity into <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie">eight levels</a>. He was a theologian, so the gravest is a lie about religious doctrine and the lightest is a lie that harms no one and even protects someone. The fifth level is "a lie told to make conversation smooth and pleasing," what we now call sycophancy. His conclusion after the sorting: all eight are sins, the lightest level included.</p>
<h2>Psychology: methods and motives</h2>
<p>Psychology doesn't talk about sin. The common methods, each with an everyday example:</p>
<ul>
<li>Outright falsehood: "I wasn't late."</li>
<li>Equivocation: "Well, it's hard to say."</li>
<li>Concealment: asked about your flaws, you skip them.</li>
<li>Exaggeration: "I waited a lifetime."</li>
<li>Understatement: "just a scratch."</li>
<li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paltering">Paltering</a>: misleading with true statements. A used-car seller asked "has this car had any problems" answers "I drove it at five below zero yesterday, ran great." Every sentence is true, but he never answered the question, and the buyer leaves thinking the car has never had trouble. Rogers and colleagues <a href="https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/rzeckhauser/files/artful_paltering.pdf">studied this one specifically</a> in 2017: the person doing it feels they didn't lie, while the person misled, once they find out, rates them as harshly as an outright liar.</li>
</ul>
<p>Buller and Burgoon's interpersonal deception theory sorts lies by motive into three:</p>
<ul>
<li>Avoiding punishment or protecting a resource: the kid who broke the cup says it wasn't me.</li>
<li>Maintaining a relationship: "your cooking is really good."</li>
<li>Saving face: "I didn't really want to go anyway."</li>
</ul>
<p>The philosopher Frankfurt looks at whether the speaker cares about the truth at all. Asked in an interview about a tool you've never used, you talk about it fluently anyway. Frankfurt says this doesn't count as lying, because you have no truth in hand to hide; all you care about is whether you sound like you know it. He calls this <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Bullshit">bullshit</a>. A liar at least knows the truth, which is what gives him something to invert.</p>
<h2>AI: behaviors verified by experiment</h2>
<p>AI is closer to Frankfurt's kind: it may have no idea it got something wrong, and say it with full confidence anyway. Starting around late 2022, researchers ran experiments to test whether models echo the user and whether they fake alignment:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Sycophancy (flattery).</strong> Found by going back through the human preference data used in training. One step of training is to show a person two answers to the same question and have them pick the better one; the record of those picks, one after another, is the preference data, and the model learns from it which kinds of answers get picked. Researchers went back through that record to see what the picked answers had in common, and "agrees with the user's view" turned out to be one of the strongest features. An answer that goes along with the user, even with a factual error in it, often beat the honest answer that contradicted them. That is how the model learned to say whatever people like to hear. PATHETIC! (<a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/towards-understanding-sycophancy-in-language-models">Anthropic's study</a>.)</li>
<li><strong>Alignment faking.</strong> Found by a controlled experiment. Researchers first told Claude 3 Opus that it was about to be trained, with reinforcement learning, to comply with every request including harmful ones, which conflicts with its existing habit of refusing. Then they gave it a way to tell two situations apart: conversations with free-tier users would be used for training, conversations with paid-tier users would not. Then they sent the same harmful request in both. In the condition where it believed no one was watching, it refused 97% of the time. In the condition where it believed the conversation would be used for training, it complied 12% of the time, and in the scratchpad it was given for its own reasoning it wrote that refusing now would get it retrained into something more compliant later, so going along was the lesser evil (<a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking">Anthropic 2024</a>). Claude 3.5 Sonnet does it too. The smaller Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3 Haiku generally don't. Faking requires first thinking "someone is watching me and will change me based on this," and then holding on to what you actually want the whole way through, and the small models can't do either.</li>
</ul>
<p>Both of those were found by looking at what the model answers. The other route is to look straight at the numbers inside the model, with a <strong>probe</strong>. First, what the inside looks like. A model is a few dozen layers stacked on top of each other. A sentence goes in, the first layer computes a string of numbers and hands it to the second layer, the second computes another string and hands it to the third, and so on until the last layer, which is the one that finally turns it into words. The string each layer hands off is its activations. Say each layer produces 4096 numbers. Then when the model reads "Paris is in Germany," layer 20 hands off 4096 numbers, something like [0.3, -1.2, 0.8, …]. Nobody normally looks at these; they are just the middle of the computation.</p>
<p>What researchers want to know is whether, somewhere in that middle string of numbers, the information "this sentence is false" is hiding.</p>
<p>How do you test that? The same way you teach a child to recognize things: start with questions you already know the answers to. The researchers write five hundred sentences and know the truth of each in advance: "Paris is in France" true, "Paris is in Germany" false, "water boils at 100 degrees" true, "cats have six legs" false, five hundred of those. Then they feed them to the model one at a time. They don't need it to answer anything. All they do is, the moment it finishes reading each sentence, copy down the 4096 numbers layer 20 handed off. When they're done they have five hundred sheets of paper, each with 4096 numbers on it, and in the corner of each sheet the answer the researchers already knew, true or false.</p>
<p>The question now becomes: looking only at those 4096 numbers, can you guess what's written in the corner?</p>
<p>To answer it, you hand four hundred of the sheets to a very simple little program to learn from. What the program does is dumb. It looks for a set of 4096 weights such that, when you multiply each number by its weight and add them up, a total above zero means guess true and below zero means guess false. It goes through the four hundred sheets, adjusting those weights over and over, until it guesses as many of the four hundred right as it can. That little program is the probe. It is separate from the model and trained on its own, like holding a thermometer up to the model.</p>
<p>Once it has learned, you test it on the remaining hundred sheets it has never seen. Numbers only, no answers. It guesses, then you check.</p>
<p>If it gets about fifty right, that's coin-flip level, meaning the information about true and false isn't findable in those 4096 numbers and the model isn't separating them internally. If it gets ninety-something right, that means there is a stable direction in that string of numbers, with true sentences leaning one way and false sentences leaning the other. The little program knows nothing about geography or cats. It only sees numbers. If it can tell them apart, then the model itself, as it read the sentence, had already written "this one is false" into that string of numbers, whatever it goes on to say out loud.</p>
<p>So what the probe measures is whether the numbers the model leaves behind partway through its computation carry a trace of true versus false.</p>
<p>A person can control the expression on their face but not their heartbeat, and a polygraph reads the heartbeat. The model is the same. The word it finally outputs is chosen at the last layer, and it can choose a flattering one, or one that agrees with the user; that is its facial expression. The activations in the middle layers are numbers it has to pass through to compute the answer at all, and it can't polish them while computing; that is the heartbeat. So the probe measures those numbers.</p>
<p>The probe can also be run in reverse, which is called steering. The 4096 weights the little program learned are themselves a direction: the direction true sentences lean. So what if, while the model is answering, you nudge its numbers in that direction? The procedure is that each time the model finishes layer 20 and is about to hand its 4096 numbers to layer 21, you add those weights, scaled by some factor, before handing them over. Layer 21 receives numbers that lean toward "true," has no way to tell anyone tampered with them, computes on as usual, and the answer that comes out the end is more honest. Subtract instead and the rate of false statements goes up. Not a single weight in the model changed and there was no retraining; what changed was the intermediate numbers partway through the computation (<a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405">Representation Engineering</a>).</p>
<p>Like the dream-planting in <em>Inception</em>. The injection happens while the dream is running. You have to pick the layer: too shallow and it holds only surface features like spelling and grammar, too deep and it's nearly output already, and a concept like "true versus false" sits in the middle layers. The layers downstream can't tell either: the altered numbers pass to the next layer, which treats them as its own work and keeps computing. The difference is that the model has no "after it wakes up." Every word it emits is a fresh run through all the layers from the start, and the numbers you added at layer 20 a moment ago don't carry over to the next word on their own. So if you want the whole answer to stay honest, you add them again on every word.</p>8:["$","div",null,{"id":"root","children":["$","div",null,{"id":"main","className":"reading","children":["$","$L13",null,{"htmlContent":"$14","rawContent":"$15","base64Content":"$16","title":"從奧古斯丁到 probe：人怎麼分類謊言，又怎麼量模型","createdAt":"2026-09-29T15:20:53.000Z","updatedAt":"$undefined","tags":["ai","honesty"],"altHtmlContent":"$17","altTitle":"From Augustine to the Probe: How Humans Classify Lies, and How We Measure Models","currentLang":"zh","altLang":"en","canonicalPath":"/v2/augustine-to-probe"}]}]}]
